The PKGBUILD defines a single source for x86_64: a `.deb` file downloaded from the official project domain `download-mem.nowledge.co`, which is consistent with the package's stated upstream. The checksum is provided via `sha256sums_x86_64`, so the integrity of the downloaded artifact will be verified during extraction — no `SKIP` or missing checksums are present.

During `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare`, only the global scope and `pkgver()` (if defined) are evaluated. Thus, sourcing this PKGBUILD and downloading the source will not execute any potentially malicious code. The operations are limited to fetching a verified `.deb` file and extracting it in a controlled manner later — both safe under the current command restrictions.

The SHA-256 checksum is provided and matches standard practice for verifying the integrity of prebuilt binaries.

The PKGBUILD retrieves a prebuilt .deb package from the project's official domain (download-mem.nowledge.co) and extracts it into the package directory. The source URL is consistent with the project's stated homepage (https://mem.nowledge.co), and the SHA-256 checksum is provided and matches the expected value for the x86_64 binary. The build process unpacks the .deb archive using standard tools (ar and tar), sets appropriate permissions, and creates a wrapper script to set an environment variable (NMEM_SERVER_BIN) before launching the binary. This environment variable points to an internal backend binary included in the upstream bundle, which is a normal pattern for Tauri-based applications.

The package also creates symlinks for upstream-provided CLI tools (nmem and browse-now), which are part of the official distribution. All operations are confined to standard packaging practices: file extraction, permission adjustment, launcher script creation, and symlink setup. There are no network operations during build or install, no use of eval or obfuscated code, and no attempts to exfiltrate data or modify system files outside the package directory. The use of a prebuilt binary is common for Electron/Tauri apps, especially when distributed by the vendor.

While the package uses a prebuilt binary (common for Tauri apps) and skips debug/strip options (justified for proprietary software), these are packaging choices, not indicators of malicious intent. The binary source is from the official domain, and the checksum ensures integrity. No evidence of supply-chain tampering or malicious behavior was found.
